```{r setup}

  readRDS(params$results_file)

}

# `h` is "has it", `n` is "is it missing": Quarto reads a second `!` inside
# `!expr` as a second YAML tag, so the negation needs its own name.
slots <- c("box_data", "summary_table", "logistic", "landing",
           "fairness_boxes", "fairness_logistic", "contested_zone_models",
           "coverage")
h <- vapply(slots, function(s) !is.null(res[[s]]), TRUE)
n <- !h

component <- spec_headline_label(spec)
min_cell <- spec_min_cell(spec)

# Captions are built here, not inline: a colon-space inside an `!expr` value
# is read as a YAML mapping and the render fails.
box_cap <- if (h[["box_data"]]) {
  sprintf(paste("%s scale score by %s band, grade %s, %d.",
                "Former ELs and the English-only group are references, not bands.",
                "The diamond is the mean; the red line is the proficiency cut.",
                "Groups with fewer than %d scores are suppressed and not drawn."),
          res$meta$subject, component, res$meta$grade, res$meta$year, min_cell)
} else "Academic scale score by ELP band"

summary_cap <- if (h[["summary_table"]]) {
  sprintf(paste("The same panel as numbers: %s, grade %s, %d.",
                "n counts everyone in the group; n scored is how many scores the",
                "statistics rest on."),
          res$meta$subject, res$meta$grade, res$meta$year)
} else "Summary statistics"

fairness_box_cap <- if (h[["fairness_boxes"]]) {
  paste("The same panel with the English-only group restricted to",
        "economically disadvantaged students. A crude filter, not a match.")
} else "SES-filtered comparison"
```

## Sample

`r res$meta$sample`

## Looking at

Where academic performance sits relative to English language proficiency, at
one point in time. Each ELP band is a column; beside them sit two reference
groups the bands are read against --- students who have already exited EL
status, and students who were never classified.

The question the figure exists for: **at what level of English proficiency
does language stop being the dominant constraint on content performance?**
If the distribution in a band clears the proficiency cut, students at that
level of English are performing on the content test the way the state expects
of anyone. If it does not, the exit threshold is letting students out --- or
holding them in --- at a level where the content test is still measuring
their English as much as their subject knowledge.

## Where each grade lands

Two readings of the same question. The **band** column is the first ELP band
whose students reach the cut at least half the time --- equivalently, the
first band whose median clears it. The **crossing** is the ELP scale score at
which a fitted logistic passes 50%. Agreement between them is the evidence;
disagreement says the answer depends on how you ask, and has to be read
against Prep 2's composition findings and Data Check 1's attrition.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-landing
#| tbl-cap: "Where each grade lands. A dash means no band reached half; the next column says how far the highest band got. Bold marks a landing at or above the band the exit threshold falls in."
#| eval: !expr h[["landing"]]
ft_check3_landing(res)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-landing
#| fig-cap: "The same, read across grades. Triangles mark landings at or above the exit band."
#| eval: !expr h[["landing"]]
plot_landing(res$landing, spec)
```

```{r}

cat(check3_landing_note(res), "\n")
```

## The fairness check

Is the bar being asked of English learners one that English-speaking peers
themselves clear? Two ways of asking, both of which change something the main
analysis holds fixed.

**(a) A comparable reference group.** The English-only column above is every
English-only student in the grade. Restricting it to economically
disadvantaged students narrows a comparison that otherwise confounds language
with poverty. The filter is crude --- this delivery carries one
free-and-reduced-lunch flag and no parental education --- and a matched
version is a later addition.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fairness-boxes
#| tbl-cap: !expr fairness_box_cap
#| eval: !expr h[["fairness_boxes"]]
ft_check3_summary(res, slot = "fairness_boxes")
```

**(b) A different bar.** The identical logistic, with the outcome swapped
from "reached the state's cut" to "reached the English-only group's own
average". If the ELP level implied by that bar sits below the one implied by
the state's cut, the state is asking of ELs something the average
English-speaking peer does not manage.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fairness
#| tbl-cap: "The state's cut against the English-only average, and the ELP crossing each implies."
#| eval: !expr h[["fairness_logistic"]]
ft_check3_fairness(res)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr h[["fairness_logistic"]]
cat(check3_fairness_note(res), "\n")
```

## Looking for

Three things, read together rather than one at a time.

1. **Where the boxes cross the cut.** The band whose distribution first
   reaches the proficiency line is the empirical answer to "how much English
   is enough for this content test" --- at this grade, in this year.
2. **How that compares to the exit threshold.** A gap in either direction is
   the finding. Exiting students below the crossing means they leave while
   the content test is still partly a language test; exiting well above it
   means the state is holding students longer than its own content standard
   requires.
3. **Whether the English-only column clears the cut itself.** If it does not,
   the bar being asked of ELs is one that English-speaking peers do not meet,
   which is a construct-validity problem rather than a threshold one. That is
   what the fairness check above tests directly.

## Interpreting it

This is a **cross-section, not growth.** A band's distribution describes the
students in it this year, not a path any student took. Students move between
bands year to year, and the students in the top band this year are not last
year's top band plus progress.

The reference columns carry most of the interpretive weight. Former ELs are
the group the exit rule has already acted on; the English-only group is the
standard the content test was built around. A band's position between those
two is more informative than its position against the cut alone.

## What is not here

All `r res$meta$panels` grade-and-subject panels are computed; the figure
draws one of them and the tables carry them all. Four things are still
absent.

**A matched English-only group.** The fairness check filters on a single
free-and-reduced-lunch flag. Propensity matching --- and, where a delivery
carries it, parental education --- would make the comparison a comparison
rather than a narrowing. This delivery has no parental-education field, so
the crude version is the ceiling here.

**The contested-zone models.** Type-gated, and this spec is Type 1: with a
single overall criterion there is no second criterion to disagree with it, so
there is no contested zone to model. A Type 2--6 state would get box plots
split by the second criterion within band, and one logistic with an
interaction presented as two predicted curves.

**Confidence around the crossings.** The logistic reports a point. A
delivery-quality answer wants an interval around it, and the intervals would
be wide wherever the crossing is already an extrapolation.

**A year dimension.** Each panel takes the most recent year the pairing is
available. Whether the landing moves year to year is a question this stage
could answer and does not yet ask.

::: {.callout-important appearance="default" icon=false}
## What this panel can and cannot say here

On simulated data this is **machinery, not a finding.** Every gap between EL
and English-only students in this simulation is a parameter of the generator,
not a measurement of anything. The figure demonstrates that the panel builds,
suppresses and renders correctly; it is not evidence about any state's
students. Run against a real delivery, the same figure is the stage's
substantive output.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="default" icon=false}
## Decide before moving on

1. Whether the crossing point, once the later passes report it across every
   grade, is stable enough to inform a threshold --- or whether it moves by
   grade in ways Prep 2 and Data Check 1 explain.
2. Whether the English-only comparison should be economically matched or
   taken whole, and on which variable, given what this delivery carries.
3. Which grades carry enough students, after suppression, to be read at all.
:::
